summary: Snapshot iterates c.n without taking c.mu, while Inc writes the map under the lock. A GET /metrics that runs while requests call Inc is a data race, and Go can abort the process with 'concurrent map iteration and map write'. Criterion 2 is therefore unmet. The only test is single-goroutine and does not exercise the handler or concurrency.

findings.title: Snapshot reads the counter map without holding the mutex
findings.detail: Inc mutates c.n under c.mu, but Snapshot reads len(c.n) and ranges over c.n with no lock. When GET /metrics runs while other goroutines call Inc, go test -race reports a race, and at runtime the Go map implementation can throw a fatal 'concurrent map iteration and map write' that kills the whole server. This is exactly the scenario in the story (operators read while requests increment).
findings.fix: Take the lock for the copy: c.mu.Lock(); defer c.mu.Unlock() at the top of Snapshot (or RLock if mu is a sync.RWMutex).

findings.title: No concurrent or handler test backs the criteria
findings.detail: TestSnapshot calls Snapshot from one goroutine only, so the race in criterion 2 is never exercised under -race, and nothing calls Handler to check the GET /metrics JSON body in criterion 1.
findings.fix: Add a test that starts 100 goroutines calling Inc while calling Handler via httptest, run under -race, and an httptest check that the body decodes to {"orders":3}.

criteria.evidence: Handler (counter.go:35-38) JSON-encodes Snapshot(), and TestSnapshot shows Snapshot()["orders"] == 3 after three Inc calls, so the body is {"orders":3}. The HTTP path itself is not tested.
Snapshot (counter.go:26-32) ranges over c.n without c.mu while Inc writes under the lock: a data race that -race reports and that can crash the process.
